hints: Compare the structures atom by atom and focus on what is lost from the central carbon between citric acid and tricarballylic acid.
Notice the central carbon in citric acid has an -OH group plus no H, while in the product it has an H and no -OH, so stage 1 must remove the -OH to form a C=C bond in Q.
Think about which reagent dehydrates alcohols to alkenes, and which reagent then adds hydrogen across a C=C bond while leaving the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups untouched.
walkthrough:
**Spot the functional group change**

Look closely at the middle carbon. In citric acid it is $\text{C(OH)(CO}_2\text{H)}$, a tertiary alcohol.

In tricarballylic acid it is $\text{CH(CO}_2\text{H)}$, just CH. The three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups are unchanged throughout.

**Work out stage 1, citric acid to Q**

To go from C-OH to CH we must first remove the OH. This is dehydration (elimination of water) to give an alkene.

$$\text{R}_2\text{C(OH)-CH}_2\text{-R} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=CH-R} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Tertiary alcohols dehydrate with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acting as dehydrating agent. So Q is the unsaturated tricarboxylic acid (aconitic acid).

**Work out stage 2, Q to tricarballylic acid**

Now we need to convert C=C in Q into CH-CH in the product. That is hydrogenation by addition of $\text{H}_2$ across the double bond.

$$\text{>C=C<} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{>CH-CH<}$$
The standard condition is $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ with Ni catalyst. It does not reduce $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups, so the acids survive.

options.A: Correct. Concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates the tertiary alcohol in citric acid to the alkene Q, then H2 and Ni hydrogenates the C=C to give tricarballylic acid. Both reagents leave the three carboxylic acid groups unchanged.
options.B: Stage 1 is correct, but stage 2 is wrong. LiAlH4 is a powerful reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols. It would destroy the three CO2H groups instead of just hydrogenating the C=C bond.
options.C: Both stages are wrong. LiAlH4 in stage 1 would reduce all the CO2H groups to CH2OH, not dehydrate the alcohol. Dilute H2SO4(aq) in stage 2 does not add H2 across a C=C bond.
options.D: Stage 2 is correct, but stage 1 is wrong. NaOH(aq) would simply deprotonate the carboxylic acids and the alcohol to form salts. It cannot eliminate water to form the alkene Q.
